heading: YŪSHAʿ IBN NŪN (AS)
title: COURAGE WITH TRUST, LEADERSHIP WITH INTEGRITY
themes: Faith • Learning • Courage • Tawakkul • Honesty • Responsibility • Service
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | QUR’AN + AUTHENTIC HADITH SOURCE LIBRARY
introduction: Volume Fifteen follows the volumes about Mūsā and Hārūn (peace be upon them) by focusing on Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn (AS), known in Islamic scholarship as the young companion of Mūsā. This world is unusually important for source literacy: the Qur’an does not name Yūshaʿ explicitly. In Sūrah al-Kahf it refers to Mūsā’s young attendant; the identification as Yūshaʿ is recorded in authentic Hadith. The Qur’an also describes two men of faith in al-Māʾidah 5:23; the widely transmitted identification of one as Yūshaʿ belongs to Tafsīr rather than the explicit verse. A Hadith names Yūshaʿ in relation to the holding of the sun. Thus the historical curriculum is intentionally shorter than that of Yūsuf or Mūsā and must never be expanded through invented childhood scenes or unsourced dialogue.

Modern fiction follows Imaan, Akhlaq, Salaam, Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle, Sir Zameer, Mohsin and Mohsina as they plan a community learning-and-service trail. These are contemporary, invented experiences, not events from Yūshaʿ’s life. The fictional journey helps children practise careful learning, completing tasks, honouring shared property, courageous cooperation and responsible leadership.

blocks.text: The old compass did not move. It lay beside the notebook where Imaan and Akhlaq had written their final lesson from the story of Prophet Hārūn (AS): “Protect the trust you are given.” On the opposite page Dadi Jaan had written a new question: WHO WAS THE YOUNG COMPANION? Akhlaq looked at the family. “I thought our next journey would have a new Prophet’s name on the first page!” Dadi brought a Qur’an and opened Sūrah al-Kahf. The verses spoke of Mūsā and his young companion, but the companion’s name was not printed there. “Then how do we know?” Imaan asked. Sheikh Uncle brought a book of Hadith. “This is why careful learning matters,” he said. “The Qur’an tells us about the journey. Authentic Hadith identifies the companion as Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. We must not pretend that the name appears in the verse.” For the school exhibition, the children made four cards: QUR’AN, HADITH, TAFSĪR and FICTION. Akhlaq was tempted to put every interesting fact under Qur’an so his display would seem impressive. Mohsina disagreed. “Truth matters more than looking clever.” The children made a new card that said: A GOOD EXPLANATION SHOWS WHERE IT CAME FROM. Later, when a younger pupil asked who Yūshaʿ was, Akhlaq answered carefully rather than dramatically. For the first time, he discovered that identifying the source was part of honouring the story itself.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Respect the difference between scripture, Hadith, commentary and fiction.

stories.title: The Companion Who Remembered
stories.subtitle: Learn, admit errors and make corrections

blocks.text: The next morning, Sir Zameer gave the children a practical task. Their group was to prepare a walking trail through the school garden for new pupils. Each path required a safe sign, and each sign needed an accurate instruction. Akhlaq took charge of a folded map. He was so excited that he forgot to mark the gate near the drinking-water station. When the others checked his map, a passage appeared to end in the wrong place. Akhlaq wanted to erase the mistake before anyone noticed. “Then it will look perfect,” he muttered. Imaan had been reading the passage about Mūsā’s young companion in al-Kahf. “The companion explained what he had forgotten,” she said. “Our garden map is only a school activity, not the sacred journey—but we can learn to admit an error.” Akhlaq told Sir Zameer the gate had been omitted and helped correct the route. “Telling me early helped the whole team,” the teacher said. They walked the route again; this time Mohsin checked entrances, Mohsina checked that younger pupils could pass easily, and Imaan read the written directions. Akhlaq added a note to his map: ADMIT IT, CORRECT IT, AND KEEP GOING. He felt embarrassed for a moment, then relieved. A good companion, he learned, need not pretend to be incapable of mistakes. A trustworthy companion speaks honestly and helps put things right.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Admit errors and help repair them.

stories.title: The Missing Detail
stories.subtitle: Distinguish authentic facts from guessed details

blocks.text: A bright poster appeared in the academy corridor: “YŪSHAʿ’S EXACT AGE AND THE DAY HE TRAVELLED.” Underneath were dates and details that none of the children recognised. Akhlaq thought the poster looked impressive. “It must be true,” he said. “It has lots of numbers.” Sheikh Uncle asked a different question: “Where did the writer find these facts?” No source had been written. Imaan searched the assigned Qur’anic passages; the dates were not there. Mohsina read the Hadith summary; the age was not there either. “We cannot use something simply because it sounds convincing,” Sir Zameer explained. He encouraged the children to write a courteous note asking for evidence, not to accuse anyone of lying. The poster’s author admitted that the dates came from an unverified online retelling. Together they removed the claims and added a clear source note. In the afternoon Akhlaq made a sorting activity. Blue cards carried direct Qur’anic claims; gold cards carried authenticated Hadith identification; white cards carried a modern class example. “Which of these proves the Prophet’s exact birthday?” he asked playfully. “None,” Mohsin replied. “So we leave it unknown,” Imaan said. Dadi praised their restraint that night. Knowledge can be honoured both by what we say and by what we refuse to invent. Akhlaq closed his notebook feeling that an empty box labelled UNKNOWN was not a weakness. It was honesty.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Do not invent facts to make a story exciting.

stories.title: Two Voices Against Fear
stories.subtitle: Courage joined to faith and wise planning

blocks.text: The school council announced that a popular path through the courtyard would be closed for maintenance. Some pupils worried that nobody would be able to reach the small reading room. Others wanted to ignore the safety notice and use the path anyway. Mohsin proposed a different route but feared people would laugh at him. Imaan remembered the two men described in al-Māʾidah 5:23 who gave courageous advice while directing their people to rely upon Allah. Sheikh Uncle carefully explained that their words belonged to a serious historical event and that the Qur’an did not name the two men in the verse. The children would not reenact an ancient confrontation. Their own decision was simple: they should obey the safety barrier and politely propose another accessible route. Mohsin spoke to the teacher. He carried a map and showed why his suggested path was safer. The teacher thanked him for thinking about younger children and pupils with mobility needs. “Courage,” said Salamah that evening, “does not mean disregarding danger. It can mean speaking responsibly when silence would leave a problem unsolved.” Akhlaq wrote COURAGE WITH CARE on the next exhibit card. For the first time he saw that gentle advice could be brave even when the speaker was unsure whether everyone would agree.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Let safe courage be thoughtful and respectful.

stories.title: A Promise to Do Our Part
stories.subtitle: Reliance upon Allah and responsible effort

blocks.text: Rain arrived on the morning of the service trail. All the children had promised to help carry books into the reading room, but the courtyard was slippery and the boxes could not be moved as planned. Akhlaq announced that they should simply give up. “We had a perfect plan, and now it is ruined.” Salaam reminded them that relying on Allah does not mean pretending we control the weather. The family prayed and considered what safe work they could still do. Mohsina suggested checking the book labels indoors; Imaan offered to organise the shelves; Mohsin could test the route once the floor was dry. Nobody tried to force the original plan through dangerous conditions. Sir Zameer connected the lesson to the Qur’anic command to place trust in Allah, while carefully explaining its own historical context in Sūrah al-Māʾidah. The children were not being compared to the people in the ancient account. Instead, they were practising a modest lesson in responsible effort. By afternoon the books were sorted and the wet pathway remained closed. “We did not complete everything,” Akhlaq said. “But we did the part we could do safely.” “That is an achievement worth noticing,” Imaan replied. Their service trail had changed shape. Their intention to help had not disappeared.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Trust Allah while doing the safe work available.

stories.title: The Work That Belongs to Everyone
stories.subtitle: Stewardship and honesty with shared property

blocks.text: A small donation box sat beside the reading corner, collecting coins for replacement storybooks. At the end of the week, the class counted the amount together with Sir Zameer. Mohsin noticed that the record did not match the count. Nobody accused anyone. They checked the earlier totals, found a copying error and corrected it. Later, when ordering books, Akhlaq wanted to reserve the nicest covers for his friends. Mohsina reminded him that the books had been donated for all students. Sheikh Uncle discussed a narration about a Prophet’s community and the seriousness of taking from collective property. “Do not turn a complex historical report into a school crime drama,” he told them, “but stewardship is a valid modern responsibility.” The children drew up a clear borrowing system: name, book, date and return place, without publishing a list of who was careless. When a book disappeared temporarily, they looked for it and asked kindly before forming any accusation. It was eventually found in the wrong cupboard. Akhlaq wrote another line on the exhibit: WHAT IS SHARED MUST BE PROTECTED FAIRLY. The greatest improvement was not a new lock. It was the habit of checking records and remembering that everyone had a right to use the books.

During an afternoon lesson, Akhlaq was fascinated by the Hadith about the sun being held for Yūshaʿ. “Can we make a game where players stop the sun by pressing a button?” he asked. Dadi Jaan shook her head. “A miracle is Allah’s act. We should not make it look like a human power, or a trick anyone can activate.” Sheikh Uncle distinguished the authentic reports for the class. One narration names Yūshaʿ, while an account in the major Hadith collections speaks of a Prophet without naming him in that wording. The teacher promised that a qualified scholar would review the exact narrations before the app displayed them. Instead of a miracle game, the children explored an ordinary timetable. They estimated how much daylight remained for a garden clean-up and chose to stop before dusk. “We cannot command the sky,” said Imaan, “but we can use our time responsibly.” Akhlaq smiled at the difference. The Hadith taught him about Allah’s power; the school activity taught him to plan within his own limits. Neither lesson needed a flashing sun-control button. At home, Akhlaq coloured a simple horizon on his notebook and wrote: ALLAH CONTROLS CREATION. I AM RESPONSIBLE FOR MY CHOICES.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Remember that miracles belong to Allah; use your time well.

The final exhibition opened quietly. Each family received a small route card marked with eight stops: evidence, honest reporting, admitting uncertainty, courage, reliance, fairness, gratitude and service. There were no gold medals for the most religious child. Parents and children could discuss a practical action privately, or simply listen. Imaan explained how the Qur’an refers to Mūsā’s young companion, while Hadith names Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. Akhlaq showed the source cards and admitted that his first poster had put every fact in the wrong category. Mohsin described the safer route through the courtyard, and Mohsina demonstrated the shared-book system. Dadi Jaan asked them to choose one lesson to carry forward. “I want to ask where a claim comes from,” Imaan said. “I want to admit mistakes before they grow,” Akhlaq answered. Mohsin chose calm courage, Mohsina chose fairness, and everyone agreed that helpful work should not become a competition. At the end Sheikh Uncle folded the trail map. He left one last card in the family notebook: WHEN GUIDANCE IS LEARNED, LET IT APPEAR IN YOUR CONDUCT. The little compass remained where it always was. They no longer needed it to shine. The next world would bring new lessons, but the habits they had practised could travel with them.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Make one ordinary habit of goodness your lasting legacy.

synthesis.text: What our sources establish

The Qur’an records Mūsā travelling with a young attendant, including the companion’s report about the fish and their return to the place sought. Authentic Hadith identifies this attendant as Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. The Qur’an also records the faith and counsel of two unnamed men in al-Māʾidah 5:23; classical commentators often identify them as Yūshaʿ and Kālib. A narration associates Yūshaʿ with the extraordinary holding of the sun by Allah. These are different types of evidence and must remain labelled accurately. Beyond these materials, we do not invent a complete biography.
Eight enduring lessons
Honour the Qur’an by quoting only what it actually says.
Reliable Hadith can clarify details without altering the wording of the verse.
It is wise to admit uncertainty rather than invent a historical fact.
A good companion listens, learns, notices and helps correct errors.
Trust in Allah accompanies responsible, safe effort.
Courage is truthful and thoughtful, not reckless.
Shared resources are a trust and deserve fair care.
Miracles belong to Allah; our own responsibility lies in the choices we make.
Family and classroom reflection

Caregivers may ask: “How do you know where a story detail came from?”, “When did you correct something kindly?”, “Who needs support in your class?”, “What could you do safely when a plan changes?” Children may choose hypothetical examples and may skip all personal questions.
